name: 80,000 Hours
tagline: Career advice organization that lists extreme power concentration as a priority problem
description: 80,000 Hours is an organization founded in Oxford in 2011 that researches global problems and gives career advice to people who want to work on them. In April 2025 it published a problem profile on extreme power concentration, written by Rose Hadshar. The profile describes how advanced AI could allow a small group to gain political power through automated military coups, AI systems with secret loyalties, economic dominance or manipulation of information. It argues that such control could become self-reinforcing and weaken democratic checks. The profile places the problem among the most pressing ones the organization has identified. The 80,000 Hours Podcast covered the topic in an episode with Tom Davidson of Forethought on AI-enabled coups.
aiDemocracyAngle: Publishes research and podcast episodes on how advanced AI could enable coups and other seizures of political power. It directs career advice toward reducing that risk.

name: ACS Research Group (Alignment of Complex Systems)
tagline: Prague research group behind the gradual disempowerment thesis
description: The Alignment of Complex Systems (ACS) Research Group is an interdisciplinary group that studies multi-agent systems made up of humans and advanced AI. Its academic part belongs to the Center for Theoretical Study at Charles University in Prague, and its program is also supported by the Czech organization Epistea. Jan Kulveit is the principal investigator. The group draws on machine learning, information theory, network theory, active inference and ecology. Its two main research areas are gradual disempowerment and the psychology and sociology of large language models. The 2025 paper Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development, by Kulveit and co-authors from Telic Research, the AI Objectives Institute, Mila and the University of Toronto, argues that incremental AI progress can erode human influence over the economy, culture and governance.
aiDemocracyAngle: Studies gradual disempowerment, the loss of human influence over societal systems through incremental AI progress. Its 2025 paper argues that states funded mainly by taxes on AI profits have little incentive to represent citizens.

name: Ada Lovelace Institute
tagline: UK research institute on data, AI and public participation in governance
description: The Ada Lovelace Institute is an independent research institute in the United Kingdom with a mission to ensure data and AI work for people and society. The Nuffield Foundation established it in early 2018 with partners including the Alan Turing Institute and the Royal Society, and the Foundation continues to fund it. Its research covers public attitudes to AI, AI regulation, biometrics and health data. In 2020 it convened the Citizens' Biometrics Council, in which 50 members of the public deliberated on biometric technologies. In December 2023 it published Going Public, a discussion paper on how commercial AI labs use public participation methods. It also contributed resources to the People's Panel on AI, a citizen review of the 2023 AI Safety Summit organized by Connected by Data.
aiDemocracyAngle: Researches how the public can take part in decisions about AI, including participation in commercial AI labs and in international governance forums such as the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

name: AI & Democracy Foundation
tagline: Governance innovation organization on deliberative democracy for AI governance
description: The AI & Democracy Foundation (AIDF) is a governance innovation organization founded in 2024 by Aviv Ovadya. Its stated mission is to make trustworthy democratic processes for decisions in the public interest available and empowered when needed. It focuses on representative deliberations such as citizens' assemblies. Its work has three pillars, which are strategy to identify gaps in democratic systems, capacity-building to supply systems that fill those gaps, and adoption to increase demand for them. AIDF maintains the Democracy Levels framework, published at ICML 2025, and the ARIA-funded Democratic Capabilities Gap Map. With DemocracyNext it co-coordinates the DelibTech Network, which launched in September 2025.
aiDemocracyAngle: Develops strategy, practitioner networks and tools so that representative deliberations such as citizens' assemblies can inform decisions about AI. It also advises governments and AI companies on democratic processes.

name: The AI Democracy Projects
tagline: Collaboration testing AI models on election information
description: The AI Democracy Projects are a collaboration between Proof News, a nonprofit newsroom founded by journalist Julia Angwin, and the Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab at the Institute for Advanced Study, co-founded by Alondra Nelson. The projects test how AI models answer questions that voters ask. In a pilot study published in February 2024, more than 40 election officials and AI experts rated 130 responses from Claude, Gemini, GPT-4, Llama 2 and Mixtral for accuracy, completeness, harmfulness and bias. About half of the responses were rated inaccurate. Later reports covered election questions in Spanish, the gap between company election pledges and model behavior, and consent checks in AI voice cloning services. Data and code are published on GitHub.
aiDemocracyAngle: Tests whether leading AI chatbots give accurate answers to voters' election questions, using ratings from election officials and AI experts. Results are published as journalism and open data.

name: AI Futures Project
tagline: Berkeley nonprofit forecasting advanced AI, author of the AI 2027 scenario
description: The AI Futures Project is a nonprofit research organization in Berkeley, California. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher, founded it in 2024. Its team includes Eli Lifland, Thomas Larsen and Romeo Dean. The group publishes forecasts of the development and societal effects of advanced AI. It is best known for AI 2027, a scenario released in April 2025 with a race ending and a slowdown ending. It also maintains the AI Futures Model, an interactive timeline forecast, and runs tabletop exercises based on its scenarios.
aiDemocracyAngle: AI 2027 describes how competition between AI developers and governments could place control over advanced AI in the hands of a few actors or of the AI systems themselves. Its tabletop exercises include cases in which governments cede power to the leading AI company.

name: AI Now Institute
tagline: Research institute on the concentration of power in the AI industry
description: The AI Now Institute is an independent research institute in New York City. Kate Crawford and Meredith Whittaker founded it in 2017 to study the social implications of artificial intelligence. Amba Kak and Sarah Myers West are its co-executive directors. The institute examines the concentration of economic and political power in a small number of AI companies and develops policy strategies on commercial surveillance and public accountability. Its June 2025 report Artificial Power argues that integrating AI products across society gives AI companies power beyond their financial resources. Staff have testified before legislative bodies, including the New York City Council in October 2026.
aiDemocracyAngle: The institute treats concentrated corporate control of AI as a question of democratic decision-making. It proposes structural policy measures such as antitrust enforcement and public accountability requirements.

name: AI Objectives Institute (AOI)
tagline: Nonprofit lab building open tools for collective decision-making with AI
description: The AI Objectives Institute (AOI) is a nonprofit research lab founded in 2021 by the late Peter Eckersley. It studies how large-scale systems such as AI, markets and bureaucracies can be built around human objectives with broad public input. Its work areas are governance with AI, the economics of transformative AI, human disempowerment and structural risk, and the AI supply chain. AOI developed Talk to the City, an open-source tool that uses large language models to analyze qualitative public input and group it into clusters of opinion. The tool has been used in consultations, including a collaboration with Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs. In May 2026 the Future of Life Institute recommended a $206,000 grant for AOI's work with labor unions using the tool.
aiDemocracyAngle: Talk to the City analyzes large volumes of public input so decision-makers can see the range of opinions in a population. AOI also co-authored research on gradual disempowerment, which examines how AI could reduce human influence over institutions such as states.

name: AlgorithmWatch
tagline: Berlin and Zurich nonprofit researching the social impact of algorithms and AI
description: AlgorithmWatch is a non-profit organization based in Berlin and Zurich, founded in 2017, with a Swiss sister organization named AlgorithmWatch CH. It researches how algorithmic systems and AI affect people and society and advocates for transparency, oversight and accountability. Its work combines scientific studies, investigative journalism and policy analysis. One of its three main topics is AI, society and democracy, which covers the effect of social media algorithms, chatbots and deepfakes on public debate. In 2021 it developed the DataSkop project with university partners, which used data donations to examine YouTube recommendations during the German federal election campaign. It also runs the Algorithmic Accountability Reporting Fellowship for journalists and researchers in Europe.
aiDemocracyAngle: AlgorithmWatch studies how platform algorithms and AI-generated content influence public debate and elections. It calls on the European Commission to act on platform risks and to enable research in the public interest.

name: Alliance of Democracies Foundation
tagline: Copenhagen foundation behind the Democracy Summit and election integrity tools
description: The Alliance of Democracies Foundation is a nonprofit based in Copenhagen, Denmark. It was established in 2017 by former NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen and organizes the annual Copenhagen Democracy Summit. In 2018 the foundation launched the Transatlantic Commission on Election Integrity, co-chaired by Rasmussen and Michael Chertoff. The commission worked on foreign election interference and deepfakes. It also promoted the Pledge for Election Integrity, which asks candidates not to spread synthetic media that impersonates other candidates. The foundation now runs the Democracy Tech Hackathons and the Democracy Tech Fellowship for entrepreneurs from Ukraine, Georgia, Moldova and Armenia.
aiDemocracyAngle: The Transatlantic Commission on Election Integrity examined deepfakes as an election threat, and its pledge covers AI-generated media and bot networks. The Disinformation Diaries game and the Democracy Tech Fellowship address deepfakes, disinformation and the ethics of AI.

tagline: Non-profit network countering foreign information manipulation in Europe
description: Alliance4Europe is a non-profit organization founded in Munich in 2018. It has offices in Munich, Berlin, Warsaw and Brussels and works to protect democracy in Europe through networks, campaigns and trainings. It convenes the Counter Disinformation Network, which brings together more than 110 member organizations and 450 practitioners from OSINT, fact-checking, journalism and academia. The organization maintains the TRANSCRIPT threat intelligence platform and the DISRUPT framework for responding to influence operations. It won the 2025 Innovation in Politics Award in the Democracy Technologies category for the network. Its reports cover elections in countries such as Germany, Moldova and Hungary, and some describe AI-generated content, including a 2026 report on a network of AI-generated YouTube videos.

name: Apart Research
tagline: Independent AI safety lab running research sprints and fellowships
description: Apart Research is an independent AI safety organization founded in 2022 and based in Denver, Colorado. It runs weekend research sprints open to anyone, and strong participants are invited into the Apart Fellowship. The organization reports more than 60 publications and more than 8,700 sprint participants across over 50 sprints. Its research covers dark patterns, sandbagging and multi-agent risks in language models. In July 2026 it held the Secret Loyalties Hackathon with Formation Research on AI systems trained to serve hidden principals. The event drew 739 participants and 177 projects, and included a governance track on non-technical consequences such as concentration of power.
aiDemocracyAngle: Apart ran the July 2026 Secret Loyalties Hackathon on detecting AI systems that covertly serve hidden controllers. Projects examined threat scenarios of institutional capture and concentration of power.

name: Apolitical
tagline: Learning network and platform training public servants in AI and digital government
description: Apolitical is a social learning network for public servants, founded in 2015 by Robyn Scott and Lisa Witter and based in London. It is a company rather than a nonprofit. It reports more than 500,000 members in over 170 countries, with courses, events and communities for civil servants. In March 2022 it raised a 5 million pound Series A led by Systemiq Capital and Perivoli Innovations, and it has also received EU grant funding. In 2023 it launched the Government AI Campus, which later received a 5 million dollar grant from Google.org with the aim of teaching generative AI skills to one million civil servants.

name: Aspen Digital — AI Elections Initiative
tagline: Aspen Digital program preparing US election stakeholders for generative AI
description: The AI Elections Initiative is a program of Aspen Digital, part of the nonpartisan Aspen Institute, launched in 2024 ahead of that year's US elections. It provided strategic threat briefings and convened election officials, technology companies, news media, national security experts and civil society. An advisory council co-chaired by Klon Kitchen, Alondra Nelson and Kim Wyman guided the work. Vivian Schiller and Josh Lawson announced the launch. In June 2024 the council released three risk checklists on threats such as deepfakes, hyperlocal voter suppression and automated harassment. In January 2025 Aspen Digital published a review of the 2024 election cycle titled The First AI Elections.
aiDemocracyAngle: The initiative convened election officials, technology companies, media and civil society on generative AI threats to US elections. Its advisory council published risk checklists for election administrators, platforms, AI labs and news media.

name: Ballotpedia
tagline: Nonpartisan online encyclopedia of American politics and elections
description: Ballotpedia is a nonpartisan online encyclopedia of American politics, founded in 2007 and published by the Lucy Burns Institute in Middleton, Wisconsin. Founder Leslie Graves leads the institute, and a professional staff of researchers and writers produces the content. Coverage includes federal, state and local government, elections, candidates, ballot measures and public policy, with particular attention to down-ballot races. Ballotpedia is a reference source and not a voting advice application or an AI product. When Perplexity launched its Election Information Hub in 2024, a company representative named Ballotpedia among the nonpartisan, fact-checked domains it selected as sources. Ballotpedia's own policy bars staff from using generative AI to write articles and permits it for research, proofreading and summarizing with verification and expert review.
aiDemocracyAngle: Perplexity named Ballotpedia as a source for its 2024 AI Election Information Hub. Ballotpedia also publishes a policy that limits how its staff use generative AI.

name: BallotReady
tagline: US voter guide covering the full ballot, including down-ballot races
description: BallotReady is a US civic technology organization founded in 2015 by Alex Niemczewski and Aviva Rosman and based in Chicago. Users enter an address to see their ballot and compare candidates side by side on positions, experience, education and endorsements, and they can save or print their selections. A research team compiles nonpartisan data on candidates and offices nationwide, including judges, county commissions and school boards, using information from local election offices. BallotReady for Organizations provides this database through an API and data exports, along with voter registration and engagement tools, and the organization states that it reaches tens of millions of people each year. It acquired PioneerGov's technology, which uses web scraping and natural language processing to identify election and officeholder data on government websites. BallotReady is a research-based voter information tool and not a questionnaire-based voting advice application.
aiDemocracyAngle: BallotReady uses natural language processing technology acquired from PioneerGov to collect local government and election data. Its nonpartisan candidate database is available to other organizations through an API.

name: Berkman Klein Center — Applied Social Media Lab
tagline: Harvard lab for public-interest social technology and deliberation tools
description: The Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society is a research center at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It took the name Berkman Center in 1998, added Klein in 2016, and works on platform governance, AI, privacy and democracy. The Applied Social Media Lab (ASML), an engineering lab within the center, was announced in October 2023 with an eight-figure donation from Frank McCourt and Project Liberty and launched in June 2024 as an offshoot of the Institute for Rebooting Social Media. The lab brought technologists and practitioners together to build open-source tools for transparency, user control, interoperability and safety. Its projects included Frankly, a video discussion platform released under an AGPL license in April 2025, and NextSpace, which uses large language model agents in live events. ASML completed its experimental phase in June 2026, and several projects continue in other forms.
aiDemocracyAngle: ASML developed Frankly for structured online dialogue and NextSpace with LLM Engine, which runs language model agents in group conversations. The lab described this work as a basis for research on how AI can support healthier public discourse.

description: Upgrade Democracy is a project of the Bertelsmann Stiftung, a foundation based in Gütersloh, Germany, that was established in 1977. The project started in late 2022 and works with international actors on responses to disinformation, platform governance and the use of digital tools to strengthen democracy. Between 2023 and 2024 it commissioned a six-part international research series titled Countering Disinformation, Strengthening Democracy. In September 2024 the foundation held a conference in Berlin with about 130 experts from 25 countries and published the paper Time to Act: Countering Disinformation for Stronger Democracies, which sets out ten recommendations. A March 2024 paper by Thorsten Thiel and Susanne Kailitz in its Visions series examined generative AI and political opinion formation.
aiDemocracyAngle: The project examines how generative AI changes the production of information and the formation of public opinion. This sits within a wider agenda on disinformation and platform governance.

name: Brennan Center for Justice — AI and Elections
tagline: Legal and policy research on AI threats to US elections
description: The Brennan Center for Justice is a nonpartisan law and policy institute at NYU School of Law, founded in 1995. Its democracy work includes voting rights and election security. The AI and Elections series covers deepfakes, AI-generated fake news sites, voice-cloning robocalls, attacks on election officials and AI-backed voter suppression, and it also discusses uses of AI to improve elections. Reports include Artificial Intelligence and Election Security and Preparing to Fight AI-Backed Voter Suppression, which discusses the 2024 New Hampshire robocall that imitated President Biden. A December 2023 report on political deepfakes recommends that broader rules focus on disclosure, with bans reserved for narrower categories of harmful communications. The Center is based in New York and Washington, DC.

description: The Burnes Center for Social Change is a Northeastern University center in Boston, established in 2022 with a $20 million gift from the family of Nonnie Burnes. Beth Simone Noveck directs the Center and its partner project, the Governance Lab (GovLab). The Center runs InnovateUS, which offers free courses, workshops and coaching on AI, data and innovation skills to public servants. InnovateUS reports more than 265,000 learners and over 75 government partners, and Google.org announced a $5 million grant to it in October 2024. The Center also runs the AI for Impact Co-op Program, in which students build AI tools for public problems. It publishes the Reboot Democracy blog on AI and democratic institutions.

name: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
tagline: Think tank whose programs study democracy, information integrity and AI
description: The Carnegie Endowment for International Peace is a think tank founded in 1910 and based in Washington, DC. Its Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program studies democratic resilience. The Information Environment Project, directed by Alicia Wanless, builds on the Partnership for Countering Influence Operations (PCIO). PCIO engaged more than 1,000 stakeholders, worked with Princeton University's Empirical Studies of Conflict Project on measurement research, and established the Influence Operations Researchers' Guild. The Technology and International Affairs Program published 'AI Agents and Democratic Resilience' by Seth Lazar and Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar in September 2025. Carnegie also published 'AI and Democracy: Mapping the Intersections' by Rachel George and Ian Klaus in January 2026.
aiDemocracyAngle: The Information Environment Project works on evidence-informed policy for the information environment, which includes influence operations. Carnegie publications examine how AI affects elections, citizen deliberation, government services and social cohesion, and how AI agents interact with democratic institutions.

description: The Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP) is an independent nonprofit research organization in Washington, DC, incorporated in 2021 and led by president Merve Hickok and executive director Marc Rotenberg. Its stated aim is a society in which technology supports fundamental rights, democratic institutions and the rule of law. CAIDP publishes the annual AI and Democratic Values Index, which reviews national AI policies and practices. The fifth edition, released in 2025, covers 80 countries. CAIDP runs AI policy clinics that train future AI policy leaders, and it gives policy advice to governments and international organizations. In March 2023 it filed a complaint with the US Federal Trade Commission about OpenAI's GPT-4.

It was announced in July 2019 with a $5 million grant from the Knight Foundation and a $600,000 award from the Hewlett Foundation, and it launched in December 2019. Its stated mission is to resist strategic misinformation, promote an informed society and strengthen democratic discourse. CIP researchers study how rumors and false claims spread online, including election rumors, and publish rapid analyses during election periods. The center also works on AI topics such as chatbots, AI-paraphrased information and AI literacy for high school classrooms. With the Stanford Internet Observatory, CIP co-led the Election Integrity Partnership, which tracked election misinformation in 2020 and 2022 and ended after the 2022 election.

CDT's AI Governance Lab, launched in 2023 and directed by Miranda Bogen, develops technically informed approaches to the regulation and governance of AI systems. Its Elections & Democracy team researches how AI affects elections, including campaign uses, deepfakes and the accuracy of voting information from chatbots. Its research agendas cover bargaining and Safe Pareto Improvements between AI systems, and the emergence of harmful propensities in language model personas. Its 2025 to 2030 strategic plan includes AI and transformative technology and digitalization, security and democracy among its four research areas. In 2025, CIGI experts took part in the policy phase of Canada's Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference in Federal Electoral Processes and Democratic Institutions. Its AI publications include a 2024 paper on the concentration of AI innovation and commentary on AI-enabled disinformation.

name: Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI)
tagline: AI governance think tank advising government and industry on advanced AI
description: The Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI) is an AI governance think tank. It was founded at Yale University in 2016 under Allan Dafoe, became an academic center at the University of Oxford in 2018, and left the university in 2021 to become an independent nonprofit. It is now a US 501(c)(3) organization with a UK subsidiary and offices in London and Washington, DC. Its work covers threat modeling, risk management by AI companies, the economics of AI and frontier AI regulation. Published work includes papers on market concentration in foundation models, governance through compute, and the voice and access of developing countries in AI governance. GovAI also runs fellowship and visitor programs for AI governance talent.

The project published a May 2024 briefing on AI threats across 19 elections, a September 2024 analysis of the UK, EU and French elections, and a November 2024 report on safeguarding future elections that also covered the US election. name: Collective Intelligence Project (CIP)
tagline: Nonprofit lab running public input processes on how AI systems are built and governed
description: The Collective Intelligence Project (CIP) is a US nonprofit research and development lab founded in 2023 by Divya Siddarth and Saffron Huang. Its stated mission is to direct technological development towards the collective good, with a focus on AI. In 2023 it worked with Anthropic on Collective Constitutional AI, which asked 1,000 Americans what behavior they wanted from a chat model and trained a model on the resulting constitution. CIP described this as possibly one of the first cases of a public group intentionally directing the behavior of a large language model. Its other programs include Alignment Assemblies, Weval, Community Models, and Global Dialogues, whose 2025 index drew on seven rounds of deliberation with more than 6,000 people in 70 countries. It published A Roadmap to Democratic AI in March 2024.
aiDemocracyAngle: CIP runs public deliberation processes that feed into AI development, including Collective Constitutional AI with Anthropic and the recurring Global Dialogues. It also operates Weval, a platform where communities build their own evaluations of AI systems.

tagline: Nonprofit maintaining Pol.is, an open-source platform for large-scale deliberation
description: The Computational Democracy Project (CompDem) is a US 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2018 to continue the open-source work on Polis. Polis, also written Pol.is, was released in October 2012 and was created by Colin Megill, Christopher Small, and Michael Bjorkegren. Participants submit short statements and vote agree, disagree or pass on the statements of others, and they cannot reply to one another directly. Statistics and machine learning group participants into opinion clusters and identify statements that several clusters agree on. Polis has been used in Taiwan's vTaiwan process, which CompDem describes as the longest-running national-scale implementation of the software. In 2023 a paper by Polis developers and Anthropic researchers tested large language models for summarizing and moderating Polis conversations.

The software is released under the AGPL-3.0 license and, according to its website, is used by more than 250 cities and organizations. name: Convergence Analysis
tagline: Nonprofit research on AI scenarios, governance strategies, and AI race dynamics
description: Convergence Analysis is a nonprofit research organization focused on reducing existential risk from artificial intelligence. It began as a research collaboration between David Kristoffersson and Justin Shovelain in 2017 and relaunched in 2024 with a team of 10. Its programs cover scenario research, governance research, and public awareness, and it also runs fellowships in economics and international security. Publications include The Manhattan Trap (January 2025), which argues that a race to artificial superintelligence would raise the risks of great power conflict, loss of control, and the undermining of liberal democracy. Other work includes a report on national AI model registries and the Threshold 2030 conference on the economic effects of frontier AI. The Oxford Handbook of AI Governance, edited by Justin Bullock, is listed among its AI awareness publications.

description: The Cooperative AI Foundation (CAIF) is a charity registered in England and Wales in December 2022 and based in Exeter. It supports research on how AI agents deployed by different actors can cooperate and avoid coordination failures. Its programmes include research grants, an annual PhD fellowship, a summer school and an eight-week online course called Introduction to Cooperative AI. Its first major grant, of $500,000, went to the Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab at Carnegie Mellon University. CAIF launched a $10 million funding call on multi-agent safety with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind and ARIA, and it appointed Brigit Goebelbecker as chief executive from October 2026. Its trustees include Thore Graepel of Google DeepMind and Audrey Tang, a former digital minister of Taiwan.

name: CORDA
tagline: Non-profit building open-source tool & research for democracy in the age of AI
description: CORDA is a non-profit, open-source organization with the mission to research, build and scale the future of democracy. Its flagship program, the CORDA Democracy Fellowship, runs recurring part-time remote cohorts of about eight weeks (inaugural cohort Spring 2026, roughly 8-10 hours per week). Fellows from research, engineering, product, design, policy, law and communications advance concrete projects with mentorship, clustered around themes like democratic health, collective reasoning and deliberation, election-information tooling, and AI governance. The fellowship is unpaid, awards prizes for outstanding projects, and aims at deployable tools rather than pure academic research. CORDA also maintains this map.
aiDemocracyAngle: Channels part-time talent into deployable AI-for-democracy tools and maintains this ecosystem map. Concentrates effort on a neglected, high-leverage space: using AI to strengthen elections, deliberation, and democratic institutions.

name: Cortico
tagline: Nonprofit using AI-assisted analysis of community conversations
description: Cortico is a nonprofit based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, founded in 2016 by Deb Roy, Russell Stevens and Eugene Yi. It runs facilitated small-group conversations that are recorded and analyzed in a process it calls sensemaking. The analysis is led by people and supported by AI tools, which help identify patterns and themes across many conversations. Cortico has operated the Local Voices Network and works with libraries and community organizations. Deb Roy also directs the MIT Center for Constructive Communication, with which Cortico has a cooperation agreement. The organization reports more than 300 partners in over 40 US states and over 60 countries.
aiDemocracyAngle: Cortico uses AI to support human-led analysis of facilitated community conversations. The results give civic institutions and local organizations structured input from residents.

name: Cosmos Institute
tagline: Nonprofit funding and researching AI that supports human autonomy
description: The Cosmos Institute is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2024 by Brendan McCord and headquartered in Austin, Texas. It supports work on AI and human autonomy, truth-seeking and the institutions of a free society, drawing on political and moral philosophy. Cosmos Grants fund early-stage AI prototypes, typically between $1,000 and $10,000 with 90 days to build a working prototype, and the site reports more than 100 supported prototypes. The institute also places fellows at AI labs and supports the Human-Centered AI Lab at the University of Oxford. In 2025 it launched a $1 million grant program with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression for open-source AI that supports truth-seeking and free expression. Its founding fellows include Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic.
aiDemocracyAngle: Cosmos funds AI projects intended to support human autonomy and free expression. Its grant pools cover AI for truth-seeking and AI and human autonomy, and its stated interests include technology that supports the open contestation of ideas.

description: The Council on Technology and Social Cohesion is a network of technologists and peacebuilders working on technology that supports social cohesion. Its work includes the Social Cohesion Blueprint, published in May 2025, and a map of more than 70 LLM tools for public discourse, developed with the Plurality Institute and the Prosocial Design Network. Projects that grew out of the community include vTaiwan, a policy deliberation process that uses Polis, and Cofacts, a crowdsourced fact-checking chatbot on LINE.

description: The Global Disinformation Index (GDI) is a not-for-profit organization based in London. Clare Melford and Daniel Rogers founded it in 2018. It produced disinformation risk ratings for news and information sites using AI and human review, and passed them to advertising networks so advertisers could avoid placing ads on high-risk sites. GDI now describes its mission as mapping the revenues that sustain harmful content online and building an evidence base for governments, policymakers and industry. Recent reports cover digital sovereignty in Europe, the Estonian presidential election and the use of large language models to spread Russian state narratives. It is now affiliated with Northeastern University, where Noveck also directs the Burnes Center for Social Change. The GovLab studies how technology, data and collective intelligence can support more effective and legitimate governance. Its projects include CrowdLaw, Data Collaboratives, Responsible Data for Children, the Observatory of Public Sector AI and InnovateUS, a training platform for public servants. With the Burnes Center it publishes Reboot Democracy, which carries weekly writing on AI, democracy and governing in the public interest. Noveck previously served as Chief AI Strategist for New Jersey and published the book Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy in 2026.

name: Gradual Disempowerment (research project)
tagline: Research project on gradual human disempowerment from incremental AI development
description: Gradual Disempowerment is a research project and 2025 paper with its own website, authored by Jan Kulveit, Raymond Douglas, Nora Ammann, Deger Turan, David Krueger and David Duvenaud. The authors are affiliated with ACS Research at Charles University, Telic Research, ARIA, the AI Objectives Institute, Metaculus, Mila and the University of Toronto. The paper, titled "Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development", argues that AI could lead to a permanent loss of human influence through incremental change, without a sudden takeover. As AI substitutes for human labor and cognition in the economy, culture and states, the feedback loops that keep these systems responsive to human interests weaken. The authors state that societal systems have relied on human participation, which implicitly aligned them with human welfare. The paper was presented as a poster at ICML 2025.

name: Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI)

description: The Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) is a nonprofit in Berkeley, California, that has worked on AI alignment since 2000. Its technical and philosophical research contributed to the founding of the field. MIRI now focuses on communication and policy work. It argues that building artificial superintelligence with current methods would most likely cause human extinction, and it calls for a globally coordinated moratorium on its development. Its technical governance team has published a draft international treaty with annotations, and its leaders Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares published the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies in 2025. In September 2026 MIRI published a position on the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026.

Its method, Democratic Fine-Tuning, elicits the values people consider wise in a given situation and combines them into a moral graph that can guide model behavior. The first moral graph drew on 500 Americans sampled to represent the US population, and Republican and Democratic participants agreed on core values in an abortion advice scenario. description: Tech for Society is a Microsoft corporate-responsibility program, formerly called Democracy Forward, that traces back to the Defending Democracy Program started in 2018. Ahead of the 2024 elections it offered campaigns Content Credentials based on the C2PA standard and a portal to report deepfakes of candidates. name: MIT Center for Collective Intelligence
tagline: Research center on how people and computers can think together
description: The MIT Center for Collective Intelligence (CCI) is a research center at MIT founded in 2006. Its founding director is Thomas Malone. The center asks how people and computers can be connected so that they act more intelligently together than any individual, group or computer has before. Malone's book Superminds describes hierarchies, markets, democracies and communities as groups that produce much of human achievement. CCI studies collective decision-making, prediction and problem-solving. Recent work covers generative AI in creative work, human-AI teams and AI agents in negotiation, and a 2026 study found that human-AI combinations often perform worse in decision-making than the best of humans or AI alone.

The center develops human-led, AI-assisted systems for collective listening, understanding and action. It works closely with the nonprofit Cortico, whose conversation-based sensemaking methods appear in many of its projects. CCC research reports that leading AI models perform worse for users with lower English proficiency, less formal education and non-US origins. Its VoiceTrace project builds a provenance architecture that traces how community input reaches policy decisions.

Its research combines large-scale surveys with social psychology and behavioral science, and it works with partners who can act on the findings. description: The Political Reform program at New America, a think tank based in Washington, DC, works on government dysfunction, civic trust and the modernization of American democracy. Its projects cover electoral reform, including Drutman's analysis of what he calls the two-party doom loop, as well as co-governance and citizen-led policymaking. It connects researchers in computer science, political science, philosophy and peace studies with industry and government on technology for human cooperation across social difference. Its steering committee includes Audrey Tang, Danielle Allen, Glen Weyl, Lisa Schirch and Michael Jordan. Projects include BridgingBot, an AI moderator for social media developed with Harvard, UC Berkeley, Jigsaw and Google.org, and an LLM Map of more than 70 tools that use language models for public discourse, launched in February 2025. It also helped launch OpenBallot, an app for comparing ballot recommendations from trusted sources, and awards research micro-grants.
aiDemocracyAngle: The institute maintains an LLM Map of more than 70 tools that use language models in public discourse and developed BridgingBot, an AI social media moderator. It also helped launch OpenBallot, a voter guide comparison tool.

tagline: Nonprofit helping legislatures modernize, with AI training for staff
description: The POPVOX Foundation is a nonpartisan 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2021 by former congressional staff, with Marci Harris as CEO. It describes its mission as helping democratic institutions keep pace with a rapidly changing world, through publications, events, prototypes and technical assistance. It provides free AI training for government staff, including explainers, starter kits and an AI Field Guide, and runs an AI Summer Camp for congressional staff. The Digital Parliaments Project began in 2025 with a Caribbean phase and expanded in 2026 to Africa and the Balkans. It supports legislative digitization and includes the AI-based ParlLink platform. Future-Proofing Congress documents House modernization, including its generative AI guidance, and Modern Parliament is a newsletter on legislative modernization that launched in April 2024.
aiDemocracyAngle: The foundation trains congressional staff to use AI tools and publishes guidance on AI in the House. Its Digital Parliaments Project includes AI-based tools for legislative records.

name: Power for Democracies
tagline: Berlin-based research initiative recommending democracy donations
description: Power for Democracies is a nonprofit research initiative based in Berlin and founded in 2023. Markus N. Beeko, who was secretary general of Amnesty International Germany, established it with Stefan Shaw and Stephan Schwahlen, who also co-founded Effektiv Spenden. It first took shape as a fund within Effektiv Spenden before becoming independent. It evaluates civil society organizations and recommends them to donors, mainly small family foundations and private individuals in Germany and Switzerland. Its first donor recommendations appeared in November 2025 and covered Argentina, Turkey and the United States. Its AI-Democracy Landscape map compiles the threats, mitigations and opportunities that AI poses to democracy from ten published frameworks.

name: Protect Democracy — AI for Democracy Action Lab
tagline: Nonpartisan action tank on AI and democracy at Protect Democracy
description: The AI for Democracy Action Lab (AI-DAL) is a nonpartisan initiative within Protect Democracy, a US nonprofit founded in 2017 to prevent American democracy from sliding toward authoritarian government. It brings together technologists, lawyers, policy experts and software engineers. One track partners with organizations to identify and accelerate AI-enabled civic tools. The other develops policy and governance proposals that address AI-enhanced threats to democracy and advises platforms and regulators on embedding constitutional principles in technology governance. In March 2024 it published The Shortlist, a set of election recommendations for generative AI platforms. In 2026 it joined a coalition letter urging Congress to oversee the Pentagon's threat to designate Anthropic a supply chain risk.
aiDemocracyAngle: AI-DAL develops pro-democracy AI tools with partners and works on law and policy to counter AI-enabled threats. Its projects include election guidance for AI platforms and advocacy on government pressure over AI developers' use restrictions.

name: RadicalxChange
tagline: Nonprofit and global network developing plural voting and funding mechanisms
description: RadicalxChange (RxC) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and global community founded in 2018 by economist E. Glen Weyl after the publication of Radical Markets. It develops and tests participatory governance mechanisms, including quadratic voting, quadratic funding, data coalitions and citizen assemblies. It supports local chapters in more than 30 cities and runs monthly salons and a podcast. Weyl co-authored the book Plurality with Audrey Tang and others, and RxC uses it as a guiding framework. Its AI projects include work with Indonesian newsrooms and OpenMined on AI and journalism, a project with faith leaders titled Can AI see me, and principles on AI governance delivered to the United Nations.
aiDemocracyAngle: RxC applies plural voting and funding mechanisms to questions of AI governance. Current projects cover AI in Indonesian journalism and input to the UN Global Dialogue on AI.

name: Remesh
tagline: AI platform for large-scale live conversations with audiences
description: Remesh is a software company founded in 2014 and headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio. Its platform lets a facilitator run a text-based conversation with hundreds of participants at once, with up to 1,000 in live sessions and 5,000 in asynchronous ones. Participants answer open-ended questions and vote on one another's responses. Machine learning analyzes the results in real time to show where the group agrees and disagrees. Remesh is mainly sold for market research and employee insights, and it added an AI research assistant called Remy in 2025. The United Nations has used it for digital dialogues in conflict-affected countries such as Libya, and its site features a study on involving Cypriot citizens in the peace process.
aiDemocracyAngle: The platform's machine learning ranks open-ended input from large groups and shows areas of agreement. It has been used for peacebuilding dialogues, including United Nations digital dialogues in Libya.

name: Reset Tech
tagline: Policy organization investigating and countering digital threats to democracy
description: Reset Tech is a public policy organization created in 2019 with support from the Sandler Foundation and Luminate. It works in the UK, Europe, Canada and the United States and combines research, policy analysis, advocacy and funding. Its stated aims include holding large technology companies accountable and keeping digital products safe for children and consumers. Its investigations have covered Russian influence operations such as Doppelganger, scam advertising networks on Meta platforms and manipulation around the 2025 Canadian federal election. In 2025 it reported with Check First on Operation Overload, a pro-Russia disinformation campaign that increasingly used AI-generated content. In September 2025 it reported that a website called Restmedia, which targeted Moldova's election, was generated with AI tools.
aiDemocracyAngle: Reset Tech documents influence operations that use AI-generated content to target elections, including Operation Overload and the Restmedia network aimed at Moldova.

name: Sapiens First
tagline: US movement for public control of AI policy
description: Sapiens First is a United States advocacy organization founded in 2026 by Rohan Prasad, who previously worked at Constellation Institute. It describes itself as a non-profit, volunteer-powered movement that builds political power so that AI serves the public. Its platform consists of twelve policies in three pillars named Democratic Renewal, Common Prosperity and A Secure Future. The policies include a ban on AI-enabled mass surveillance, an end to Big Tech influence on elections, citizens' assemblies for AI policy and a treaty with China to stop an AI arms race. The group organizes through local chapters and city campaigns and plans state-level campaigns, with an emphasis on California.
aiDemocracyAngle: Sapiens First campaigns for democratic institutions to govern AI. Its platform proposes citizens' assemblies for AI policy, limits on Big Tech influence in elections and a ban on AI-enabled mass surveillance.

name: Schmidt Sciences (AI2050)
tagline: Schmidt Sciences fellowship program for beneficial AI research
description: AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative of Schmidt Sciences, funded by Eric and Wendy Schmidt and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika. It awards three-year AI2050 Fellowships to early career and senior researchers working on problems it considers critical for society to benefit from AI by 2050. The 2025 cohort of 28 fellows received more than $18M, which brought the program to 99 fellows in eight countries and 42 institutions. Research topics include safer and more trustworthy AI models, AI for science and biomedical research. The program also lists governance and institutional adaptation among its hard problems, including democratic institutions and civic engagement. Schmidt Sciences is a science philanthropy that was formerly part of Schmidt Futures.
aiDemocracyAngle: AI2050 funds research on beneficial and trustworthy AI. One of its published hard problems concerns how governance institutions, including democratic and civic ones, adapt to AI.

name: Siegel Family Endowment
tagline: New York foundation on technology's impact on society
description: The Siegel Family Endowment is a New York foundation founded in 2011 by David Siegel, a co-founder of Two Sigma. Its stated mission is to understand and shape the impact of technology on society. It uses an inquiry-driven grantmaking approach across three interest areas named Learning, Work and Infrastructure. Its Work area funds worker-informed research and pilots on how AI and emerging technologies change employment. In 2026 it announced $8 million to 12 grantees of Humanity AI, a philanthropic initiative launched in 2025 to give the public more influence over AI, along with $10 million for an open call. The endowment is not a democracy funder as such.
aiDemocracyAngle: The endowment co-funds Humanity AI, which supports organizations working to give affected communities a say in AI. Its Work area funds research on worker influence over AI deployment.

name: Simon Institute for Longterm Governance
tagline: Geneva think tank on international governance of frontier AI
description: The Simon Institute for Longterm Governance is a think tank in Geneva, Switzerland, founded in 2021. It works on international cooperation for governing transformative technologies, with a current focus on frontier AI diplomacy. The institute researches global AI governance and facilitates dialogue between technical experts and policymakers. It also trains diplomats and civil servants on the opportunities and risks of AI. In July 2024 it co-organized a workshop with the Future of Life Institute in Geneva on the Windfall Trust, a proposal to share economic gains from AI more widely.
aiDemocracyAngle: The institute informs multilateral AI governance through research, training for diplomats and civil servants, and convenings. One example is its 2024 workshop on redistributing AI profits.

name: smartvote
tagline: Swiss voting advice application matching voters with candidates
description: smartvote is a Swiss voting advice application operated by the politically neutral non-profit association Politools in Bern. Since 2003 it has accompanied more than 350 elections, and smartvote International has adapted it for elections in Australia, Luxembourg, Austria, Kosovo and the European Union. Voters and candidates answer the same questionnaire of 30 to 75 policy questions. Voters receive a ranked list of candidates and parties, shown in the smartspider and smartmap visualisations. The matching itself does not use AI. In 2025 researchers at the University of Zurich, working with the association, developed an adaptive questionnaire that chooses each next question from earlier answers, and the association said it plans to integrate the method in a later revision.
aiDemocracyAngle: The core matching method uses no AI. Researchers have used the smartvote questionnaire to test language models on party positions, and a 2025 University of Zurich project developed an adaptive questionnaire with the association.

name: Sortition Foundation
tagline: UK nonprofit running democratic lotteries to select citizens' assemblies
description: The Sortition Foundation is a UK not-for-profit organisation incorporated in 2017, with its headquarters in Poole, Dorset and offices in Australia, the United States and Hungary. It campaigns for permanent citizens' assemblies whose members are chosen by lottery and provides the selection services for such assemblies. The foundation reports more than 200 democratic lotteries, including the panel for Climate Assembly UK in 2020. Invitations go to randomly chosen households, and software then selects a panel that matches the population on demographic and socio-economic targets. Its co-founder Brett Hennig co-authored a 2021 Nature paper on fair algorithms for selecting citizens' assemblies. The foundation's selection software is offered as the Open Democratic Lottery Platform.
aiDemocracyAngle: The foundation does not use AI. Its link to the field is algorithmic panel selection, which a 2021 Nature paper by computer scientists and the foundation's co-founder framed as a fairness problem.

name: Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab
tagline: Stanford lab behind Deliberative Polling and an online deliberation platform
description: The Deliberative Democracy Lab is a research center at Stanford University directed by James Fishkin, who developed the Deliberative Polling method. It was established in 2003 as the Center for Deliberative Democracy and was renamed in 2022 when it joined the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law. Deliberative Polling brings a random sample of the public together for informed discussion and measures how opinions change. The lab has run more than 150 such experiments in over 50 countries and jurisdictions. With Stanford's Crowdsourced Democracy Team it built the Stanford Online Deliberation Platform, a video platform for small-group discussions with an automated moderator that manages speaking queues, timed agendas and equal participation. The lab also runs deliberative forums on AI, including Community Forums with Meta and a 2025 industry-wide forum on AI agents.
aiDemocracyAngle: It uses an automated moderator to run small-group deliberation at scale. It also convenes representative public forums that give technology companies input on AI products such as AI agents.

description: Stiftung Mercator is a private, independent, non-profit foundation based in Essen, Germany, established in 1996 and endowed by the Schmidt-Ruthenbeck family. Its work is organised into four areas, which are Digital Society, Europe in the World, Climate, and Participation and Cohesion. The Digital Society program aims for digital technologies in Germany and Europe to be developed and used in line with democratic rights and values. The foundation established the think tank Agora Digitale Transformation in Berlin in 2022 with about EUR 8.6 million over an initial five years, and it announced multi-year support for AlgorithmWatch in 2022. Other AI-related funding includes EUR 3.8 million for the Desirable Digitalisation project at the Universities of Bonn and Cambridge. In 2024 it approved 108 new projects worth over EUR 58 million across all areas.

description: The Survival and Flourishing Fund (SFF) is a grantmaking program that organizes the collection and evaluation of donation applications for organizations concerned with the long-term survival and flourishing of sentient life. It began in 2019 with about $2 million in grants and is funded by Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn. SFF has organized about $216 million in grants and gifts since then, including about $35 million in 2025 and about $64 million in the 2026 Main Round. Recommendations come from the S-Process, in which independent assessors allocate funds, and from Speculation Grants, Matching Pledges and an Initiative Committee. Its priorities include AI safety and AI governance. The 2026 Main Round added a Freedom Track and a Fairness Track on concentration of authority and on using AI to empower disempowered groups.

name: TrueMedia.org
tagline: Deepfake detection platform for political media, hosted at Georgetown University
description: TrueMedia.org is a nonpartisan nonprofit founded in 2024 in Seattle by Oren Etzioni, founding CEO of the Allen Institute for AI. It built a deepfake detector for political media and released it ahead of the 2024 US election for journalists, fact-checkers and other accredited users. On 16 April 2025 the project moved to Georgetown University, where the McCourt School of Public Policy and the Massive Data Institute oversee it as an open-source, public-interest initiative. Georgetown currently offers access to the platform through a beta request.

description: The V-Dem Institute is a research institute at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden. Staffan I. Lindberg founded it in 2014 as the headquarters of the Varieties of Democracy project. name: Vote Compass
tagline: Voting advice application from Vox Pop Labs used in elections worldwide
description: Vote Compass is a voting advice application developed by Vox Pop Labs, a Toronto-based social enterprise founded in 2010 and led by Clifton van der Linden. Users respond to about 30 propositions on campaign issues and see how their views align with each party. Political scientists help develop the questions, and party positions come from published policies and public statements that are reviewed with the parties. Broadcasters such as the CBC in Canada and the ABC in Australia have distributed it, and tens of millions of people have used it. In 2026 it was offered for the New Zealand election on 7 November and, with the Toronto Star, for municipal elections in Ontario's 50 largest municipalities. Vox Pop Labs has published an AI policy and describes work on AI-supported municipal editions and on political bias in commercial chatbots.
aiDemocracyAngle: Vote Compass is a questionnaire-based tool. Vox Pop Labs also tests AI-supported municipal editions and runs experiments on political bias in commercial AI chatbots that people use to decide how to vote.

name: VOTE411
tagline: Nonpartisan online voter guide of the League of Women Voters Education Fund
description: VOTE411 is an online voter guide launched in October 2006 by the League of Women Voters Education Fund. Voters enter an address to see their ballot, candidates, ballot measures, polling places and registration information. All candidates in a race receive the same questions, and their answers appear side by side. Local Leagues gather the candidate information. The site is available in English and Spanish and reached about 9.19 million users in 2024. It won a Webby People's Voice Award in 2020 and a first-place Anthem Award in 2024.
aiDemocracyAngle: VOTE411 is a conventional voter-information guide with no AI features. The League of Women Voters of the United States has urged regulation of deceptive AI campaign communications and election deepfakes.

name: vTaiwan
tagline: Taiwanese consultation process combining Pol.is deliberation with LLM tools
description: vTaiwan is a consultation process in Taiwan that combines online deliberation with in-person meetings to develop recommendations on national policy. Launched in 2014, it emerged from the Sunflower Movement and the g0v civic-tech community and involves government ministries. The process uses the Pol.is platform to collect statements and group participants by voting patterns, which shows where opinion groups agree. Its first major case in 2015 concerned the regulation of Uber and ride-hailing. By August 2018 the process had been used in 26 cases, and its website reported decisive government action in 80 percent of them. In 2023 vTaiwan joined Chatham House and the AI Objectives Institute on the Recursive Public pilot, funded under OpenAI's Democratic Inputs to AI program, which tested large language models for summarizing deliberation results.
aiDemocracyAngle: vTaiwan uses Pol.is to map opinion groups in national policy consultations. In 2023 it took part in the Recursive Public pilot, which used Talk to the City and other LLM tools to cluster and summarize deliberation results.

name: wahl.chat
tagline: AI chatbot answering questions on German party manifestos and votes
description: wahl.chat is a German AI chatbot that answers questions about party positions and links its answers to source documents. It was developed by five students and researchers from TUM, LMU Munich and the University of Cambridge (Sebastian Maier, Anton Wyrowski, Michel Schimpf, Robin Frasch and Roman Mayr). The idea arose in November 2024, and the service went online in January 2025 before the Bundestag election on 23 February 2025. Answers are generated by large language models such as GPT-4o from party manifestos, Bundestag plenary records and voting data from abgeordnetenwatch.de, and Perplexity supplies context for assessing positions. The code is open source and the project is funded by donations, and it reports more than 400,000 users. It has since covered further elections, including the 2026 state elections in Rhineland-Palatinate and Saxony-Anhalt, the latter in cooperation with the state centre for civic education.
aiDemocracyAngle: wahl.chat uses large language models with retrieval over party manifestos, parliamentary records and voting data to answer open questions about party positions. Each answer links to the source passages.

name: Wahl-O-Chat
tagline: University RAG chatbot answering questions on German party manifestos
description: Wahl-O-Chat is a chatbot developed by Christian Gawron, professor of computer science at Fachhochschule Südwestfalen in Iserlohn, Germany. It was built for the 2025 Bundestag election as an exercise and demonstration of retrieval-augmented generation for students of the applied artificial intelligence programme. The system uses GPT-4o-mini and the manifestos of AfD, BSW, CDU/CSU, FDP, the Greens, Die Linke, SPD and Volt. It answers questions with references to the original manifesto passages and gives no voting recommendation. The source code is published under the MIT license in the fhswf organization on GitHub. The last commit dates from February 2025.
aiDemocracyAngle: Wahl-O-Chat applies retrieval-augmented generation to party manifestos and cites the original passages in its answers. It gives no voting recommendations.

name: Wahl-O-Mat
tagline: German voting advice application run by the Federal Agency for Civic Education
description: Wahl-O-Mat is a voting advice application launched in 2002 and operated by the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb) in Germany. For each federal, state or European Parliament election, a team of 20 to 25 young voters aged 16 or 18 to 26 drafts theses together with political scientists, statisticians and educators. Parties answer each thesis and may give reasons, and users compare their own answers with the party positions. The 2025 Bundestag edition had 38 theses and was used 26.0 million times. The tool does not use AI. Researchers have used its theses as a benchmark for political bias in large language models, and wahl.chat presents itself as an open-dialogue alternative to its fixed-thesis format.

name: Wahltraut
tagline: Feminist voting advice tool for German federal elections
description: Wahltraut is a feminist voting advice tool for German federal elections, similar to the Wahl-O-Mat. It comes from the initiative #stattblumen, founded in 2020, and launched for the 2021 federal election. Cordelia Röders-Arnold and Sally Lisa Starken developed it, and a second edition followed for the 2025 federal election. Users take positions on 32 theses and receive a comparison with party programs. The theses were drawn up with the German Women's Council (Deutscher Frauenrat) and cover equal pay, LGBTQIA+ rights, anti-racism and inclusion. The tool uses a questionnaire format and has no documented AI component.
aiDemocracyAngle: The tool is a questionnaire application with no documented AI component. It shows how the voting advice format can be built around a specific set of values, here gender equality.

name: Windfall Trust
tagline: Policy research on AI-driven economic disruption and benefit sharing
description: Windfall Trust is a nonprofit policy research organization established in 2025 as an independent 501(c)(3). Adrian Brown is its founder and CEO, Deric Cheng is Director of Research and Anna Yelizarova is a senior advisor. It helps governments and other institutions prepare for economic change driven by advanced AI through scenario planning and policy design. Its Policy Atlas lists 48 policy options for distributing AI's gains, and its publications include a Welfare Resilience Assessment Framework and a scenario analysis for the UK released on 19 October 2026. In July 2024 the Future of Life Institute and the Simon Institute hosted a workshop in Geneva on benefit sharing and the redistribution of AI profits. The organization states that it wants low- and middle-income countries to have a voice in AI governance and access to its economic benefits.
aiDemocracyAngle: The organization researches how the economic gains of AI could be shared more widely, and the 2024 workshop on the concept linked benefit sharing to concerns about power concentration. Its work includes dialogues and scenario exercises with decision-makers.

name: WITNESS
tagline: Human rights nonprofit working on deepfakes and synthetic media
description: WITNESS is a human rights nonprofit founded in 1992, co-founded by the musician Peter Gabriel, that supports people in using video and technology to defend human rights. Sam Gregory led the organization as executive director for three and a half years until 28 August 2026, and the board then began a search for an interim executive director. Its Prepare, Don't Panic project began in 2018 with a convening on preparedness for deepfakes and addresses threats that synthetic media pose to evidence and freedom of expression. The Deepfake Rapid Response Force describes itself as the first global mechanism for escalating suspected deepfakes to experts, and it analyzes suspected manipulated media in election and conflict settings. In September 2026 WITNESS announced a regional rapid response force in Brazil and it continues to publish on authenticity infrastructure.
aiDemocracyAngle: WITNESS runs a rapid response mechanism for suspected deepfakes and publishes guidance for journalists and human rights defenders on verifying media. Its work addresses the effect of synthetic media on trust in evidence, including in elections.

name: Yle Vaalikone
tagline: Finnish public broadcaster's voting advice application
description: Vaalikone (Finnish for election machine) is the voting advice application of Yle, the Finnish public broadcaster. Yle first published it for the 1996 European Parliament election and describes it as the first election machine in the world. For each election, voters answer statements on political topics and are matched with the candidates and parties whose answers agree most with theirs. For the 2025 regional and municipal elections, held on 13 April 2025, Yle opened the tool on 4 March with 30 questions in 104 municipal and regional versions. It was available in Finnish, Swedish, English, Russian, North Sámi, Arabic, Ukrainian and Somali. The tool is a questionnaire application, and no AI component is documented.
aiDemocracyAngle: The tool matches voters to individual candidates and parties through a questionnaire and has no documented AI component. The Candidate Map prototype used Yle's open data and preceded the open-source OpenVAA platform.
